809c97251106670b: KUALA LUMPUR: Tempoh reman empat pegawai tentera udara (TUDM) bagi membantu siasatan sindiket pengedaran dadah menggunakan kemudahan pengangkutan tentera disambung empat hari lagi bermula esok hingga 28 Nov.
Pengarah Jabatan Siasatan Jenayah Narkotik (JSJN) Bukit Aman Hussein Omar Khan berkata, tempoh reman pertama kesemua pegawai terbabit selama tujuh hari sejak 18 Nov lepas tamat hari ini.
Katanya, seorang lagi pegawai tentera yang ditahan di Labuan dan tempoh reman pertamanya selama lapan hari berakhir esok turut akan dimohon sambungan reman pada hari sama.

Selain itu, polis akan memohon sambungan reman terhadap dua orang awam yang ditahan di Labuan serta dua pegawai tentera udara yang ditahan di Tawau, Sabah, apabila reman selama tujuh hari terhadap mereka tamat Jumaat ini.

“Pada masa sama, empat orang awam yang ditahan di Cheras, di sini, telah ditangkap semula bagi membantu siasatan kes melibatkan TUDM itu dan direman tujuh hari bermula hari ini hingga 30 Nov,” katanya.
Minggu lepas, Hussein memaklumkan polis berjaya membongkar sindiket pengedaran dadah yang menggunakan kemudahan pengangkutan tentera menerusi operasi di Lembah Klang dan Labuan.
Dalam operasi itu, polis merampas 96.64kg dadah disyaki jenis methamphetamine (syabu) bernilai RM4.83 juta serta 6.98kg cecair bahan kimia.

Menteri Pertahanan Khaled Nordin sebelum ini memaklumkan, penahanan itu susulan penemuan dadah yang disembunyikan dalam lima bagasi dan sebuah kotak di Bangunan Pergerakan Udara, Pangkalan Udara Subang.

Dadah berkenaan dikesan menerusi pemeriksaan rutin terhadap barangan sebelum dimuatkan ke dalam pesawat TUDM, sekali gus menjadikan kejadian itu kes pertama seumpamanya berjaya dipatahkan menerusi prosedur pemeriksaan berkenaan.
b759104e87b208ea: PETALING JAYA: PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang claims the Islamic party is seeing growing support from non-Muslims who are not comfortable with DAP, which he labelled as extreme.
Speaking to reporters in Parliament, Hadi said PAS was confident of defeating Pakatan Harapan in the next general election (GE16), based on the "encouraging" outcomes of recent state elections.
He also pointed to the poor turnout of delegates at the Selangor DAP convention over the weekend, which drew a rebuke from party secretary-general Loke Siew Fook.
“God willing, we can defeat PH. Look at the 2022 general election (GE15) results, as well as the results in Melaka, Negeri Sembilan and Johor.
“These are good signs. It means even non-Muslims are no longer supporting DAP. They disagree with extremism, such as that practised by DAP," said Hadi.
DAP suffered a wipeout in the 2025 Sabah state election and lost several key seats in the Johor and Negeri Sembilan polls, where Loke lost his Chennah seat.
The party managed to retain its four seats in Melaka during the Nov 14 state election, but lost the contest in three other seats.
At the Selangor DAP convention, Loke said the party was in “crisis mode” and needed to change its approach and develop new strategies.
He said DAP appeared to have grown complacent and lost the fighting spirit it had when Pakatan Rakyat captured Selangor in 2008.
GE16 talks with BN later on
Separately, Hadi said seat allocation between Perikatan Nasional and Barisan Nasional for GE16 would be announced closer to the election date.
Asked about how seats in the three PAS-led states would be distributed, Hadi said it was too early to comment on the matter.
"God willing there will be no problem, whether it's a PAS or Umno candidate contesting. Wait for GE16," he said in sidestepping the question.
Analysts previously said the BN-PN pact would have a tough time agreeing on the distribution of parliamentary seats in Perlis, Kedah, Kelantan and Terengganu, where Umno was wiped out in GE15.

02a5577b695a8b93: KUALA LUMPUR: A government backbencher has cautioned Putrajaya against allowing foreign companies to operate data centres in Malaysia, arguing it may not be economically beneficial to the country.
Teresa Kok (PH-Seputeh) pointed out that between 2021 and mid-2026, some 117 data centre projects had been approved, with an investment value of RM386 billion.
She, however, did not provide a breakdown of data centres owned by foreign companies.

“We cannot allow ourselves to become landlords (to data centres) who offer cheap utilities and land resources to house servers owned by foreign companies,” she said during the committee-stage debate on the digital ministry's 2027 budget.
Kok also claimed that data centres did not generate many job opportunities.

"Since these centres started operating, they function like quiet automated warehouses with only a handful of technicians,” Kok said, alluding to the 55 data centres – which are part of the 117 projects – that are up and running.

“More worryingly, we are taking on an enormous financial risk to meet the projected data centre energy demand by 2030,” she said, noting Tenaga Nasional Bhd’s plans to invest RM90 billion over the next six years to upgrade its electrical grid infrastructure to better handle energy demand from data centres.
Kok said borrowing this amount at a 4.8% interest rate would result in annual interest payments of RM4.32 billion.
She added that the energy demand was expected to account for 21% of Malaysia's electricity demand by 2030.
She went on to compare the data centre industry with the country’s semiconductor sector which had captured revenue of RM400 billion in 2025.
Kok said, however, that only 40% of the export value remained in Malaysia, with the rest of the profits moving abroad.
“We cannot fall into the same trap with data centres.”
fbc9f17566894033: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly.

Speaking at a press briefing on Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm.

The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution.

Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday.
"There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said.

The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities.

The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred.
The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points.
The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data.
The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient.

"I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority."

The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing.

The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns.
More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers.
"As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®
6e57439c0e5b3d97: NEW YORK: Russia's war against Ukraine may reach a tipping point next year that leads to a defeat for Moscow, Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics told Reuters, citing Russia's worsening economy and growing international pressure.

Rinkevics, in New York to chair the United Nations Security Council during Latvia's rotating presidency, said he did not believe Moscow was genuinely interested in ending the war and likely viewed fresh negotiations on a ceasefire as a "decoy" to continue its full-scale invasion.

Ukraine was facing a "perfect storm" of a brutal winter, increased attacks against energy infrastructure and escalating strikes against civilian targets, but Europe was standing by to help Kyiv with military, financial and infrastructure support and Ukraine had repeatedly proven its resilience, he said.

"If we see Ukraine surviving from a military point of view, from an economic point of view - and I'm sure Ukraine is going to survive - then the tipping point could be next year, next spring, next summer," he said in an interview recorded on Monday.

In addition to pressure on Russia's economy, there was growing political consensus about the need to end the war, Rinkevics said, citing attacks that had killed Indian sailors or struck ships from the Philippines and others.
"The number of countries that are putting pressure is going (up) so the tipping point may come in spring, summer, next year," he said, noting that the war was widening beyond the immediate region.

He also expressed concern about what he called increasing "hybrid activities" which have been directed against European countries and that are likely linked to Moscow, including airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage.
Russia has been careful thus far not to cross the red line of triggering an Article 5 declaration under Nato that would force members to come to each other's aid, but is growing bolder, he added.

"From what we see now, Russia is very, very careful (not) to breach this threshold. At the same time, there is another tendency: the appetite for risk is growing in Russia," he said, noting that the number of sabotage activities, arson attempts and attacks against Ukraine-friendly entities was up sharply from 2022, when Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.

Recent hybrid incidents in Germany, Spain and the Baltics - some of which are still under investigation - posed challenges in terms of determining a proportionate response, but Europe's intelligence agencies are improving their ability to cooperate and coordinate, preempting attacks in some cases, Rinkevics said.
The Kremlin consistently denies conducting sabotage operations ⁠in Nato countries or plotting any confrontation.

Latvia on Monday again summoned Russia's ambassador in Riga over recent Russian attacks, Rinkevics said, underscoring the importance of such public rebuke at the same time that European countries were fighting back with "more cooperation, more intelligence sharing, more mutual support."

"That's the result of very good cooperation across intelligence and counterintelligence community," he said. "The trouble always is that you always have a very skilled enemy that is also implementing new ways of trying to test you and trying to attack you, and this is ongoing fight."

Apabila syarikat itu berpindah ke Kuala Lumpur, Samad turut berpindah dan membantu Usman menguruskan majalah Mastika. Samad kemudian berkhidmat sebagai ketua bahagian pengembangan sastera di New Straits Times.
Pada 1987, beliau melepaskan jawatan editorial di Berita Harian untuk menumpukan sepenuh perhatian kepada penulisan, khususnya esei dan puisi.

Samad juga aktif dalam kegiatan sosial dan politik, memainkan peranan penting dalam Gerakan Mansuhkan PPSMI pada 2009, yang membantah pengajaran sains dan matematik dalam bahasa Inggeris, serta menyertai perhimpunan Bersih 2.0 dan 3.0 bagi memperjuangkan reformasi pilihan raya.

50dc6ec5c93f6b80: A software fault cut short BepiColombo's Mercury orbit insertion burn, but the European Space Agency (ESA) says the mission remains on track to separate its two science orbiters on December 9.

ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), still carrying JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), fired its four axial thrusters on November 21 to place the spacecraft in orbit. The burn began at 1824 UTC, when BepiColombo was approximately 635 km above the planet's surface. It was supposed to last for 37 minutes but shut down early.
The shutdown, caused by a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, left the spacecraft in safe mode, a protective state in which all non-essential activities cease.
Ignacio Tanco, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Operations Director, said: "Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened."
The burn achieved around 77 percent of the planned velocity change, securing an orbit around Mercury but leaving BepiColombo taking 75 hours to circle the planet instead of the intended 58.

The good news is that multiple burns were always going to be needed to adjust the orbit ahead of Mio separation and MPO reaching its science orbit. "The remaining MOI [Mercury Orbit Insertion] sequence has already been adapted to the new trajectory, with no additional burns required," ESA said.
"After each burn, the Flight Dynamics team determines the achieved orbit to then design the next manoeuvre," said Frank Budnik, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Dynamics Manager.

"So, the sequence is not only more propellant-efficient, it also allows Flight Dynamics to adapt each subsequent burn to the spacecraft's actual trajectory. It's a dynamic sequence! Each new manoeuvre is based on the previous ones."
Teams at ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) and Airbus continue to investigate the underlying software fault.
ESA has not said whether the revised burn sequence will affect propellant reserves available for a possible mission extension.
The separation of Mio and MPO is planned for December 9, and more burns will be needed to guide MPO to its final orbit by March 2027, with science operations starting in April 2027. ®

84edfb5a38475599: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

311a6446282aa440: PETALING JAYA: Petronas Chemicals Group Bhd’s (PCG) turnaround took a breather in the third quarter after it reported lower earnings from the preceding quarter amid softer overall average product prices.

The petrochemical group posted a net profit of RM179 million for the quarter ended Sept 30 (Q3 FY2026) from a net loss of RM289 million a year ago while revenue rose 12% to RM7.62 billion, according to its bourse filing today.

Net profit for the first nine months of FY2026 rose to RM994 million against a net loss of RM1.39 billion a year earlier when it booked foreign exchange losses and wrote down the value of assets at its Swedish specialty unit Perstorp.
Nine-month revenue was up nearly 8% year-on-year to RM22.54 billion as higher selling prices outweighed lower sales volumes and a stronger ringgit that cut into export receipts.

On a quarter-to-quarter basis, Q3 earnings were significantly lower as product prices fell, particularly for urea, a widely used fertiliser. Urea prices fell to US$407 per tonne from US$667 per tonne in the second quarter.

Profit after tax tumbled 54.6% to RM202 million from RM445 million in the second quarter. Third quarter revenue was down 4% to RM7.6 billion from the preceding quarter mainly due to lower average product prices despite higher sales volume from its Pengerang operations and strategic sourcing.

“The third quarter was marked by softer product prices across the portfolio, with urea particularly affected by increased export availability from China,” said managing director Mazuin Ismail in a statement.
Petronas Chemicals said its plants were operating at 73% of capacity in Q3, with utilisation reaching 90% in October following turnaround activities.
Its shares closed unchanged at RM3.82 today, giving the group a market capitalisation of RM30.56 billion. The stock is up 5.2% year to date.

Its shares surged nearly 105% to RM6.13 on March 30 after the US-Iran war ignited and Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, driving up petroleum and petrochemical prices. The stock had been trading at RM3.00 just before the war started on Feb 28.

Petronas Chemicals was seen as a prime beneficiary of the crisis as it gets its feedstock supplies from within Malaysia rather than the Middle East. However, the stock has given up much of its gains in recent months.

The group is the chemical arm of national oil company Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas) and is one of Southeast Asia's largest integrated chemical producers. It operates 21 manufacturing sites and 54 production plants.

63f90f482b3d4aaa: InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Plan 9 from Bell Labs.

For us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part. It describes the project as a "Secure Runtime for AI Agents," but we think it's something far more interesting than another LLM tool.

Fair warning: this vulture has no interest whatsoever in AI agents, and we are not even going to look at this planned use of InferNode. We're interested in the OS, and here, its GitHub repository spells out the part that caught our attention: "a 64-bit Inferno® OS."
That grabbed us because Inferno is a very interesting OS, although it doesn't get much attention – for example, the official Inferno GitHub repository shows little activity in the last few years.
Inferno is the successor to Plan 9, which we've written and talked about before, including recent releases of its community continuation, 9front.

Plan 9 is what the team who invented Unix did next. Plan 9 is a very minimalist, natively clustered Unix: machines can freely mount one another's filesystems, display windows on one another, and start processes on one another. Plan 9 turns a network of machines running this Unix-like OS into a single machine. So, for instance, if you were working on a laptop with limited storage and compute power, you could compile a large complex project on a faster machine elsewhere on the network, using project files located on a third machine, while watching the process in your terminal on your screen, with no messing about with SSH sessions.

Plan 9 and 9front programs are compiled into architecture-specific native binaries. Different processor families can still work together across the network, but the same executable won't run unchanged on both an x86-64 laptop and an Arm64 server.

Inferno takes a different approach. It's contemporaneous with the far less ambitious Java. On Inferno, languages compile code for a VM called Dis, which is part of the kernel. This means that Inferno binaries execute directly on anything that the Inferno kernel runs on. The OS kernel is built to run bare-metal, or as a process on various other OSes, without needing a separate hardware virtual machine or hypervisor.

A single binary can run on all supported CPU architectures. Inferno applications are normally written in the Limbo programming language, whose documentation was written by Unix co-creator Dennis Ritchie. Limbo is one of the languages that influenced Go, but Inferno lets compilers for other languages target Dis as well. The binaries run anywhere. Inferno on Arm, or x86, or RISC-V, or running in a Windows or Linux or macOS process, your program just runs.

We've been trying to contact Vita Nuova, the company that maintains Inferno, for some years without success. Development appears to have slowed considerably. Moving the runtime to 64-bit also raises compatibility questions: some forks change Dis's word size and cannot run existing 32-bit bytecode unchanged.

We're aware of several efforts to build 64-bit versions of Inferno. Caerwyn Jones's Inferno64 is one of the more visible, and the GitHub repository (and indeed his X account) show considerable activity. However, Inferno64's Dis is not compatible with 32-bit Dis code. Another fork is Dinsmoor's Inferno64, which also shows recent activity, albeit with the assistance of the Claude LLM. Others include the long-quiescent Purgatorio and 9ferno, both inactive for years, plus Scott Guyon's more active fork. Dropping the compatibility goal altogether, Node9 replaces Limbo with Lua and Dis with LuaJIT.

There are more forks and variants than we've gone into here. Given that there have been quite a few efforts, and most haven't delivered final ready-to-use products yet, we were surprised when InferNode was suddenly announced on the Inferno-OS mailing list last week.

Developer Peter Finn said: "An experimental runtime for containing generative AI agents was the original motivation, but most of the work since has been on the OS itself, and the AI parts are ordinary file servers. For example, llmsrv at /mnt/llm and speech9p are started from the login profile, and if you delete those lines they're simply not there. There's also non-generative AI additions on object detection served as files at /mnt/vision, on the CPU or a GPU host, and voice calls between devices done by mounting each other's audio files over 9P. There's a GUI layer intended to facilitate hands-free AI agent use, but it too is optional."

He also said that InferNode's development was largely independent of the existing efforts, partly because the primary target was Arm64, not x86-64. Its 64-bit Dis runtime is incompatible with the 32-bit original: "The opcodes, file format and magic number are unchanged, but the word size isn't, so frame sizes, offsets and pointer maps all differ. Limbo source recompiles without edits. A 32-bit .dis is currently rejected at load time."

InferNode doesn't implement 9front's DP9IK authentication protocol, so it cannot connect to servers requiring that authentication. Dr Finn told us: "DP9IK is not quantum-safe. That's the reason. InferNode's current crypto policy is strict CNSA."

InferNode also includes some slightly unexpected components, related to its intended use for testing LLM agents – such as a wallet for the Ethereum cryptocurrency, which Finn said was "mainly to support agent payments."

The first release of Inferno was in 1996, the year after Java and the JVM were launched. Inferno is a much more ambitious project, but its core function – the ability to run identical binaries on multiple platforms, without recompilation – was close enough that they ended up competing in the market, and Java won. It was a pleasant surprise to see a modernized version of Inferno arrive this year, 30 years on.

Finn told us: "About a year ago I saw the potential for a 'break-out' moment for this tech as a runtime for containing AI agents. The flood of cybersecurity risks we would face on account of adversarial AI agents required new systems with small footprints and minimal attack surfaces. Inferno was a perfect candidate and it was an opportunity to show the world how visionary Plan 9's ideas were and how well they mapped on to pressing contemporary security issues."
"If InferNode succeeds, it is an opportunity for Plan 9's ideas to migrate out of hobby-land and really make an impact – as they deservedly should."

He has a point. On a related note, this vulture discussed the possibility of rebuilding the world's IT systems from scratch on last week's Kettle podcast. Perhaps the hour for tools like this really has come round at last. ®

aedbdcad395cddbc: SEOUL: US chip giant Nvidia's customers and suppliers in South Korea and Taiwan welcomed Jensen Huang's return as CEO on Tuesday, saying it dispelled uncertainty over product plans and the risk of scaling back investments in AI startups.
Asia is home to key companies in Nvidia's sprawling supply chain such as TSMC, Foxconn 2317, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, as well as startups backed by the AI chip company.
"Without Huang, the next-generation products would have taken longer to develop," said Ahn Ki-hyun, an executive with the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association.
"Uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's next-generation products has eased," Ki-hyun said.

Many in the industry saw Huang as a major driving force behind the rapid pace of the AI boom, as he pushed Nvidia to accelerate product cycles and spurred suppliers to keep up, while also investing in promising early-stage companies.
"'Can you make it faster?'" was Huang's first question whenever he met Chey Tae-won, the chairman of SK Group, parent of memory chip maker SK Hynix, said in September.
Some plans backed only by words

An employee at one South Korean chip supplier said Huang's departure had put a question-mark over the new management's approach to plans previously agreed with Huang, particularly since some had rested on verbal agreements alone.

"With Huang back, at least from a public relations perspective, both internally and externally, the message is that Nvidia's strategy remains unchanged," said Daniel Yu, co-founder and CEO of Taipei-based MetAI, a startup backed by Nvidia.

"It will certainly help restore confidence," added Yu, whose firm builds digital twins for industrial projects, adding that Huang's departure had fuelled anxiety over how its ties with Nvidia might change.

An official at a South Korean firm in talks to receive funding from Nvidia said it had worried the US firm might become more cautious and scale back investments in an area Huang had personally championed.
"But now that he is back, I think the ecosystem has a chance to regain momentum," the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the matter is a sensitive one.
Stock markets welcome the return
Asian stock markets rallied on the news of Huang's return, with Taiwan's benchmark soaring 9% from an eight-month low and South Korea's KOSPI jumping 6%.
TSMC, Nvidia's main contract chip manufacturer, and assembler Foxconn both jumped nearly 10% to their daily limits.
South Korean chip suppliers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix also jumped, while Hyundai Motor, which works with Nvidia on automated vehicles and a data centre, rose 10.5%.
Suppliers LG Electronics and Doosan jumped 16% and 14% respectively.
However, some analysts cautioned that Huang's comeback did little to disperse the scrutiny of Nvidia, particularly regarding its China ties and concerns aroused in Washington.

"The controversy is far from over," said Sunny Cheung, analyst at Washington-based think tank Jamestown Foundation, pointing to Congressional concerns likely to spur further investigations when the new legislature gathers in January, as well as one by California’s attorney general.
"His return doesn’t make the national security concerns disappear," Cheung said.
Curbs on China chip sales likely to stay
Chinese stocks lagged the powerful global rally, as investors bet Huang's return would do little to ease US curbs on sales of advanced chips to China.
"The White House-backed reinstatement effectively ties Nvidia more closely to the US national security framework," said Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone in Melbourne.
"This could mean tighter enforcement of export controls through intermediary markets in Southeast Asia," Wu said.
China's foreign ministry declined to comment on Huang's return.
1dd18e81ee97d983: The British government is investing in a UK-based AI defense startup that aims to train autonomous military systems in virtual environments, in a bid to reduce the country's reliance on overseas technology.

"AI is rapidly transforming how wars are fought, from the use of drones through to how rapidly soldiers can interpret battlefield information. The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era," he stated. ®

7315e960f6bc4f8a: More than 355,000 school staff and pupil email addresses ended up in the hands of hackers who broke into UK education software supplier Bromcom in September.

The breach was added to Have I Been Pwned on Monday, revealing that 355,051 unique email addresses were caught up in the incident. The data also included single sign-on (SSO) registration reference numbers, although Bromcom insists that no passwords or authentication tokens were stolen.

As The Register reported in October, the attackers got in through a legacy SSO registration component in Bromcom's Communications Server environment. The technology had already been superseded but was still running because an internal system continued to use it.

Bromcom discovered something was amiss on September 6 after customers reported problems accessing its SSO service. At the time, the company was still working with external forensic specialists to establish exactly what the intruders had managed to get their hands on.
Bromcom's FAQ says its investigation is complete and confirms that the intruders used a script to extract SSO registration information from the compromised server.

The supplier insists its Management Information System (MIS), used by schools to keep track of everything from attendance to pupil records, was untouched. The compromised service also couldn't be used to get into Microsoft or Google accounts, which have their own login systems.

Bromcom has since pulled the plug on the old component, tightened its authorization checks, and added more security logging. It says it hasn't found any evidence of accounts being hijacked as a result of the breach.

Bromcom also confirmed it hadn't reported the breach to the UK's Information Commission's Office. Its reasoning is that it was the data processor, not the controller, so any decision to involve the regulator was for the affected schools and academy trusts to make.

As for the risk to staff and pupils, Bromcom considers it to be low. No passwords or pupil records held in the MIS were taken, it says, although schools have been advised to watch for phishing messages and suspicious requests to reset passwords or approve sign-ins.
The supplier's software is used by more than 5,000 schools and 390 multi-academy trusts across the UK, though it hasn't said how many were caught up in this particular mess.
The Register has asked Bromcom how many schools and pupils were affected, and whether the figure published by Have I Been Pwned matches its own findings, but has yet to receive a response.
Bromcom kept the superseded component running because an internal system still needed it. Unfortunately, the intruders found a use for it too. ®

60e8aadceb71593e: From Ann Teoh
Today marks exactly 10 years since Amri Che Mat went missing.
A Suhakam public inquiry unanimously concluded in 2019 that Amri was a victim of enforced disappearance – specifically by state agents, namely the police's Special Branch.
It was past 11pm on Nov 24, 2016, a Thursday, when Amri drove out of his house at Padang Behor in Kangar, Perlis, to have supper with a friend.
Just minutes later, less than a kilometre from his house, his Toyota Fortuner was boxed in by three four-wheel-drives. Screeching sounds, glass breaking, and that was it. It took less than a minute.
Providence would have it that the incident was witnessed by a passing motorcyclist and a restaurant owner across the road from where it happened.

Amri’s Fortuner was found abandoned at a construction site in Bukit Chabang, Kedah, a few hours later. His wife, Norhayati Ariffin, did not realise Amri hadn't come home until the next morning when she received a call about the abandoned car.
Before Amri took a nap at 7.30pm, he had asked his wife to wake him up at 10.30pm. That was the last time Norhayati saw her husband.
This sounds like a bad conspiracy novel, but reality is stranger than fiction.

DNA swabs were taken from the Fortuner when the car was found, but were sent to the chemistry department only five months later. Amri’s family also did not get the police support they wanted. Instead of trying to locate Amri, Norhayati was queried about her husband’s involvement in Shia activities.
Shia Islam is prohibited in Malaysia and Amri was watched by religious authorities and the police, but was never arrested or charged. Instead, he disappeared.
How do we know Amri was being watched? Would he have disappeared at a different time if he didn’t go out that fateful night? It's quite possible judging by the circumstances.
A car workshop owner across Amri’s house later testified that unknown cars, with engines running, took turns parking outside Amri's house day and night for three days before he went missing.
One of those cars was a gold-coloured Toyota Vios with a Penang number plate, which was also spotted when Pastor Raymond Koh was abducted 81 days later.

The Vios belonged to an operative of the Special Branch in Kuala Lumpur. He was identified as Saiful Bahari Abdul Aziz, but the police always had an excuse for why the key witness could not be present to testify.
Koh was abducted the same way on Feb 13, 2017. His car was also boxed in as men in black rushed out from three black four-wheel-drives. There was also a gold-coloured Vios nearby.

Koh’s abduction was more audacious than Amri’s; it happened in broad daylight on a Monday morning in SS4, Petaling Jaya. Amri’s case only had eyewitness accounts but Koh's case included video evidence.
Besides witness Roeshan Celestine Gomez, a chambering student who happened to be driving behind Koh's car, the pastor's abduction was caught on the CCTV cameras of two houses nearby.

Strangely, the police didn’t rush to get the CCTV recordings. It was Koh’s family who looked for them once they knew about Roeshan’s police report. After the CCTV recordings were spread through the media, the case couldn't be hidden any longer.

With two Malaysians abducted this way – and Joshua Helmi and Ruth Sitepu also missing since end-November 2016 – and a growing suspicion they were abducted, a group of civil society groups sent a memo to Suhakam seeking action.

Suhakam then carried out public inquiries on both Koh and Amri’s disappearances. Amri’s case took Suhakam 10 months to complete starting from January 2018, with 27 days of hearings and 24 witnesses summoned.

Suhakam's final reports said evidence pointed to Amri and Koh being forcibly abducted by the Special Branch. It also stated that in both cases, the police failed to investigate the disappearances properly.

The Cabinet then set up a special task force in 2019 to look into the matter. Its report in 2020 stated that it was “highly probable that Amri’s disappearance was caused by rogue police officers acting alone or in a group with unidentified individuals from religious groups".

Three years after Amri disappeared, Norhayati, who became a single mother to their four daughters, sued the police and government for malfeasance and failure to investigate his abduction properly, among others.

The civil suit filed on Nov 18, 2019, took six years, partly because the government initially refused to release the special task force's report. By the time the High Court made its decision, nine years had passed since Amri disappeared.

On Nov 5, 2025, the High Court awarded Norhayati general and exemplary damages totalling RM3 million, and another RM14,457.52 mainly for the children’s education expenses. The court also ordered a re-investigation into Amri’s disappearance.

Justice Su Tiang Joo said the police breached their own SOPs, citing severe delays in handling DNA evidence, failure to investigate the Vios owner, and failure to investigate CCTV recordings, among others. The police also made almost no effort to keep the family updated.

Su said Norhayati’s mental anguish, pain and suffering included having to dissolve her marriage under fasakh – as advised by the Perlis religious affairs department – “to bring succour to the needs of the four daughters".

Norhayati was unable to get welfare aid as a single mother if she remained married to Amri. Secondly, the divorce dispensed of the need for Amri to be a wali for one of their daughters who was getting married.
Perhaps it was to be expected that the attorney-general would appeal the High Court decision. With that, the award was stayed while Norhayati and her daughters continue to wait.
Today, we want to remember Amri.
Whatever wrongs he allegedly committed, Amri deserves a fair chance at defending himself in a court of law.
That’s the basic minimum of a modern democratic society proclaiming the supremacy of the constitution and rule of law as two of its five Rukun Negara tenets.

Abducting Amri was cowardly and dastardly because the government has the machinery, laws, institutions and manpower resources to frame a legal case against him and prosecute him, if he indeed did wrong.
The police chose a shortcut instead, and the executive arm of the government allowed that shortcut. This was a betrayal of the rakyat's trust.
Today, we remember Amri Che Mat, a Malaysian, a father of four girls (now grown women), and surely, a friend to many through his NGO, Perlis Hope.
Ann Teoh is an FMT reader.

9c8bf06abbbe421e: Complaints include marriage disputes, unfair trial, unlawful land grabs, corruption, torture, and more
Originally published on Global Voices
An old man in the Talas province addressing Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov during a public meeting. Photo from the Presidential Administration's website. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In October and November 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s president, Sadyr Japarov, held public meetings with the population in all seven provinces of the country. What were meant to be formal events turned into quests for justice by people driven to desperation.
The meetings revealed the ineffectiveness of the existing justice mechanisms and showed how people saw the president as the only guarantor of justice.

The effectiveness of Kyrgyzstan’s law enforcement and judicial bodies was people’s most common justice-related complaint. During a meeting with residents of the southwestern Batken province on October 11, a woman complained to the president about her former husband, who accused her of forging their marriage certificate and framed her for crimes she did not commit to avoid the division of assets after their divorce.

She also said her former brother-in-law provided false testimony to back up his brother’s accusations. She now lives in an apartment with their three children in constant fear that her former husband may kick them out because he allegedly bribed police and courts.

This trivial legal dispute reached the point where the woman had to beg the president to ensure a just investigation and ruling. Japarov condemned her former husband and said that he should have left everything to her and their kids after the divorce.
Here is an Instagram reel with his response to the case.
View this post on Instagram

On October 26, Japarov met with residents of the Kazarman district in the southern Jalalabad province, where Shirimbek Abrahmanov told the president about his father, who was imprisoned for allegedly offering a bribe of KGS 2,000 (USD 23) to a police officer during a traffic stop. The district court acquitted him of the charges.
However, the local prosecutor’s office appealed the decision in the provincial court, which found Abdrahmanov’s father guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison.
Here is an Instagram reel with the complaint and Japarov’s response.
View this post on Instagram
Japarov could not hide his anger when he heard the story, especially after finding out the provincial court took seven months to issue a verdict. In reply, he confronted local authorities and said:

Are the traffic police officer and the prosecutor in cahoots? Does that mean they’ve ganged up on him? If it were a large bribe, that would be one thing. But to have someone imprisoned over two thousand soms — that’s a disgrace.
The man was released from custody shortly after Japarov’s intervention and subsequent pardon.
Similar complaints resurfaced multiple times during presidential meetings in other provinces, highlighting systemic problems plaguing the judicial and law-enforcement systems.
The message is clear: people have lost all hope of finding justice at the hands of local police and courts.

Surprisingly, following his meetings with the public, Japarov concluded that the level of distrust towards courts has decreased, but admitted that problems in the judicial system remain and must be solved quickly.

On the one hand, the lack of justice and the dysfunction within the courts and police bodies, which are plagued by corruption and bureaucracy, are real pressing issues affecting millions of people across Kyrgyzstan. However, the current political regime led by Japarov, who came to power in October 2020, has made little tangible progress.
In 2026, Kyrgyzstan was ranked 99th out of 144 states in the Rule of Law Index compiled by the World Justice Project. For comparison, in 2020, it was ranked 87th.

On the other hand, people’s desperate appeals for justice helped Japarov sustain his man-of-the-people image. By listening to people’s requests and swiftly resolving their issues, the president can reinforce his popularity. In turn, this leads to the maintenance of the personalistic regime built around Japarov since his arrival to power.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

637817716fa5fe63: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond at all.

Hunt gave Anthropic’s Claude access to an email inbox containing over eight years of his email correspondence and then asked the AI to write a post summarising them, a method he said “was the best way to highlight the behaviors I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts.”

Writing in person, Hunt described those behaviors as “standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers.”

Once Claude takes over writing duties, it opens with the observation that Hunt sent his standard notification email to 73 organizations between March 2018 and November 2026 and also used website contact forms.
Claude/Hunt focuses on the breach notifications that don’t go well, for example when first contact “often goes nowhere” because “many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident.”

Some organizations Hunt contacted logged his notifications as customer support requests. “In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received,” Claude wrote, before observing “A message that an organization’s customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.”

Once someone at victim organization gets the message, a common response is to say they can find no evidence of the breach. Others try to play down the incident, saying it was only a website defacement or that Hunt is re-reporting a previous breach the victim has already disclosed.
If an organization accepts Hunt is probably onto something, it typically says it needs to investigate the matter.

Claude’s take on Hunt’s mails suggests he responds by pointing out that this is an irresponsible approach, because while the investigation takes place, “people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.”
Next, victims send in the lawyers who ask if their employer or client is legally required to reveal the breach.

Hunt typically replies by saying it is up to the victim to decide if the incident meets the threshold that triggers mandatory disclosure requirements under local laws, but that he intends to notify HIBP users regardless.
Victims don’t like hearing that and respond in three ways:
Calling to discuss disclosure, rather than committing to it;
Asking to see the wording HIBP will use in its disclosure, a request that sees Hunt refer the victim to the HIBP site for examples of the thousand-plus breach reports already on the site;
Arguing that disclosure, not the breach, is the real harm.

Hunt/Claude suggests that each argument victims use to avoid disclosure “sounds reasonable on its own,” but argues “Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.”
The post also reports on some better interactions, such as a small booking platform that was initially skeptical about Hunt’s report, then admitted he was right and acted swiftly to inform customers.

A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys, and published a disclosure. “Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency,” according to the Claude-generated text.
The bot’s analysis also offers examples of when breach notifications go well.

“Someone with authority over security answered quickly,” Claude concluded. “They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.”

Hunt appears to have asked Claude to offer its opinion of his email trove. “I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal,” the post states. “It's about incentives. For the organization, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines.”
Hunt also said he won’t make a habit of having AI write his content, but said Claude “absolutely nails it!” Unlike many of the orgs Hunt contacted. ®

048f15b5fe3e2ca2: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws.

Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources.
Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders.

The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch.
With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things:
The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux;
Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed.

“Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production.

Shirudo is open source and available here. The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation.

Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls.
Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source, and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it.

That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®

97bbc033a9e9fa11: A president’s absence and a president’s disqualification are two different things. Malaysia Athletics must establish what its constitution requires when an incumbent becomes ineligible to hold office.
World Athletics has disqualified Karim Ibrahim. He has not appealed against the decision, and the international governing body has not lifted the sanction.

Article 13.2.8 of Malaysia Athletics’ endorsed constitution sets out the consequence. It makes a person ineligible to be nominated, elected, appointed or hold office if he has been disqualified, removed or suspended by Malaysia Athletics, the Olympic Council of Malaysia, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics or another local or international sports authority or organisation.
That ineligibility continues until the relevant authority releases the person from the sanction or he succeeds in an appeal.
Karim’s disqualification therefore makes him ineligible to hold office under this provision. Malaysia Athletics must formally record it and address the consequences for the presidency.
The issue now is not the existence of the sanction, but how the association applies its own constitution to the leadership position it has affected.
The deputy president’s authority needs a clear basis
Malaysia Athletics deputy president Wan Hisham Wan Salleh now regards himself as the acting president. But the constitution must provide a sound basis for that position.

Article 12.2.2 allows the deputy president to chair Malaysia Athletics meetings when the president is absent. It also allows him to assume the president’s rights and duties at those meetings, as designated by the president.
The clause deals with the president’s absence. It does not expressly state that the deputy president automatically becomes acting president when the incumbent is disqualified from holding office.
Nor does it spell out how the deputy president should assume the full responsibilities of the presidency in those circumstances.
That difference cannot be brushed aside.

A president who is away or unable to attend a meeting may still hold office. Disqualification raises a different issue: the incumbent is no longer eligible to occupy the position under Article 13.2.8.
Wan Hisham’s claim to be acting president therefore needs more than an assumption that the deputy president naturally takes over.
The council must identify the constitutional provision, decision or other valid authority that supports his position.

Article 12.2.2 may provide for the deputy president to perform certain duties during the president’s absence. But the wording supplied does not, by itself, establish an automatic succession process after disqualification.
It also does not expressly give the deputy president a mandate to serve as acting president until the next election.
This is where the executive council must do its work. Article 18.1 gives it sole authority to interpret the association’s constitution and by-laws.
It must examine the relevant provisions together, determine what they require and record its decision.

That interpretive power does not allow the council to create a succession rule that the constitution does not contain. It must apply the written provisions, not stretch them to fit an administrative arrangement.
The council should examine Article 12.2.2 alongside Article 13.2.8 and any other clauses dealing with vacancies, removal from office, an acting president or fresh elections.
If another provision sets out the succession process, the council must follow it. If the constitution leaves the position unclear, it should obtain legal advice before deciding how to proceed.
Wan Hisham has said he will brief the executive council at its Nov 29 meeting. He has declined to answer legal and constitutional questions while awaiting legal advice.
The meeting offers the council a timely opportunity to consider the disqualification, clarify the authority under which the association is operating and decide the next steps.
It should leave no doubt about who holds the presidency, what powers that person may exercise and which constitutional provisions support the arrangement.
Other decisions need scrutiny, not sweeping conclusions
The council must also consider whether Karim’s disqualification affects decisions and appointments made during his time in office.
It should not assume that every decision made under his leadership is now invalid. Equally, it should not treat every appointment as beyond question.
Each case requires a review of the relevant eligibility rules, appointment process and circumstances.

The same care applies to the annual general meeting and the election of office-bearers. Karim’s disqualification does not, by itself, invalidate the entire meeting or the positions of everyone elected.
Any challenge must rest on the relevant constitutional provisions and the facts surrounding the election.
Members may also ask whether they can table a motion of no confidence in the current leadership.
The constitution’s provisions on notice, meetings, voting and removal must determine whether they can do so and what effect such a motion would have.
A vote of no confidence does not necessarily remove an office-bearer unless the rules provide for it.
The council should answer these questions by referring to the constitution, not through informal assurances or political agreement.
Members need to know which rules apply and how the association intends to enforce them.
Malaysia Athletics cannot afford further uncertainty over who has authority to lead it and where that authority comes from.
The association must record Karim’s disqualification, establish the status of the presidency and identify the proper process for filling the position.
It must also clarify the deputy president’s powers while that process unfolds.

If the constitution requires an election, the association should follow the prescribed procedure. If it provides another route, the council should explain and apply it. Either way, members must be able to trace the decision to a clear constitutional provision.

This is not a contest between Karim and Wan Hisham, or an opportunity for one faction to gain an advantage over another. It is a test of whether Malaysia Athletics can govern by rules rather than assumptions.
The executive council has the authority to interpret the constitution. It also has a duty to apply it fairly, consistently and transparently.
A constitution cannot be stretched to suit the people who happen to hold office. It exists to govern them, especially when leadership is in dispute. The Nov 29 meeting should make that clear.

Kita perlu memikirkan perkara yang hendak disampaikan, mencari perkataan yang sesuai, menyusun ayat, memadankan rima serta membina pembayang. Semua itu dilakukan hampir serentak. Belum lagi kalau pantun itu perlu dijawab apabila ada yang menjualnya.

Otak perlu bekerja untuk memahami maksud yang disampaikan oleh orang lain, merumuskan jawapan dan menterjemahkan jawapan itu dalam bentuk puisi yang mempunyai peraturan tertentu. Ini bukan mudah. Cuma, selama ini kita lihat pantun seolah-olah dipermainkan dan dijadikan bahan lawak sahaja dalam rancangan hiburan atau persembahan komedi. Kita kena serius sekali-sekala.

Dalam bidang pendidikan, kita sering bercakap tentang pemikiran kritis. Kita mahu anak-anak kita mempunyai kemampuan menganalisis, mentafsir, membuat perkaitan dan menyelesaikan masalah secara kreatif. Menariknya, sebahagian daripada kemahiran berfikir itu sudah lama dilatih oleh nenek moyang kita melalui suatu kegiatan yang hari ini sering kita anggap sekadar hiburan.

Bukanlah bermaksud syarat hendak berpantun mestilah mempunyai pemikiran kritis yang tinggi. Tetapi proses mencipta pantun itu sendiri memerlukan beberapa kemahiran mental yang amat berguna dalam membentuk pemikiran seseorang. Pantun juga ada tingkatannya. Ada pantun yang mudah, sekadar memadankan bunyi di hujung baris. Ada pula pantun yang pembayangnya mempunyai hubungan makna dengan maksud yang hendak disampaikan. Lebih tinggi lagi apabila pencipta pantun menggunakan perlambangan alam untuk menyampaikan falsafah kehidupan. Contohnya pantun ini:-
Yang kurik itu kundi, Yang merah itu saga; Yang baik itu budi, Yang indah itu bahasa.

Betapa ekonomisnya penggunaan bahasa dalam menyampaikan suatu pemikiran. Tak perlu panjang berjela, empat baris sahaja sudah cukup untuk membicarakan nilai kemanusiaan. Orang Melayu dahulu memerhatikan alam. Mereka melihat tumbuh-tumbuhan, haiwan, sungai, laut dan perubahan cuaca. Daripada pemerhatian itu, mereka membina perlambangan dan menghubungkannya dengan kehidupan manusia. Ini bukan sekadar persoalan penguasaan bahasa. Ini juga persoalan keupayaan membuat perkaitan antara dua perkara yang pada zahirnya kelihatan tidak mempunyai hubungan. Kemampuan membuat perkaitan inilah yang dimaksudkan sebagai salah satu ciri pemikiran kreatif.

Menteri pendidikan patut beri perhatian yang serius akan kemahiran yang sudah lama kita miliki ini. Pantun bukan sekadar diajar sebagai salah satu bentuk puisi tradisional dalam mata pelajaran bahasa Melayu semata-mata tetapi dijadikan kegiatan yang melatih anak-anak berfikir secara spontan. Adakan sesi jual beli pantun di dalam kelas. Seorang pelajar mengemukakan persoalan dalam bentuk pantun dan seorang lagi menjawabnya juga dalam bentuk pantun. Biarkan mereka belajar sambil berseronok walaupun pada permulaannya mungkin mutu pantun masih rendah. Lama-kelamaan sudah tentu pelajar akan jadi mahir serta tangkas seperti pantun lama ini:
Limau purut lebat di pangkal, Batang mengkudu condong uratnya; Hujan ribut dapat ditangkal, Hati yang rindu apa ubatnya?

Perhatikan kehalusannya. Jika anak-anak kita mampu mencipta pantun sebegini bermakna mereka telah memahami falsafah hubungan perasaan manusia dengan fenomena alam. Hujan ribut yang dahsyat sekalipun masih dianggap mampu ditangkal, tetapi kerinduan yang tidak kelihatan itu belum tentu mampu diubati.

Bayangkan juga jika seorang guru sains meminta anak muridnya menerangkan sesuatu konsep sains melalui pantun. Sudahlah perlu memahami konsep itu, mereka perlu pula memikirkan cara menyampaikannya dalam empat baris. Tentulah ada yang secara sinis mempersoalkan mengapa perlu menyusahkan diri sedangkan penerangan biasa lebih mudah. Inilah yang saya maksudkan sejak awal lagi ia bertujuan untuk mencabar kemampuan minda. Contoh lucunya ialah mamat-mamat sado yang mengangkat besi di gimnasium pun boleh kita tanyakan soalan yang sama. Mengapa bersusah payah mengangkat besi berat sebab lepas itu letak semula besi tersebut di tempat asalnya. Tapi kita segera faham yang dia sedang melatih ototnya, manakala orang yang berpantun pula sedang melatih akalnya.

Dalam zaman kecerdasan buatan hari ini, kita boleh meminta komputer menghasilkan puluhan pantun dalam beberapa saat. Tetapi tujuan mengajar anak-anak berpantun bukanlah semata-mata untuk mendapatkan pantun yang indah. Yang lebih penting ialah proses mental yang dilalui untuk menghasilkan pantun tersebut. Kita tidak mahu sekadar melahirkan generasi yang tahu mendapatkan jawapan. Kita juga mahu melahirkan generasi yang tahu bagaimana hendak berfikir untuk mendapatkan jawapan. Bertuahnya kita ialah kita sudah ada kaedah yang praktikal dalam hal ini tetapi kita kesampingkannya. Orang tua kita dulu apabila berpantun macam, GhatGpt. Prompt saja terus keluar jawapan.

Satu lagi keistimewaan pantun ialah kemampuannya menyampaikan teguran secara halus. Orang boleh berselisih pendapat, menyindir, menegur, malah berbahas tanpa semestinya menggunakan bahasa yang kasar. Dalam zaman manusia begitu mudah memaki hamun di media sosial, alangkah menariknya jika mereka perlu berpantun dahulu sebelum mahu bergaduh. Sekurang-kurangnya ada tapisan sedikit sebelum menghina orang. Kedengaran mungkin lucu, tapi kita lihatlah hari ini berapa ramai mengalami kemurungan akibat dimaki hamun di media sosial. Barangkali ada yang akan membatalkan hasrat untuk bergaduh kerana terlalu sibuk mencari pembayang. Lihatlah ketika Ahmad Maslan berpantun. Bunyinya tenang sahaja tetapi 'makan dalam'. Berbanding beberapa Ahli Parlimen yang gemar menjerit dan bertempik sehingga penyokong sendiri pun naik malu.

Kita patut berbangga dengan warisan budaya kita. Namun, kebanggaan itu tidak seharusnya terhenti pada usaha memelihara bentuknya semata-mata. Kita juga harus menggali kebijaksanaan di sebalik penciptaannya dan mencari bagaimana ia boleh dimanfaatkan dalam kehidupan moden. Pantun bukan sekadar khazanah bahasa. Ia juga khazanah pemikiran. Nenek moyang kita bukan sahaja mewariskan keindahan berbahasa, malah suatu kaedah untuk melatih ketangkasan akal.

Kalau kita sendiri kurang menghargai keistimewaan pantun, tahukah kita bahawa hampir dua abad dahulu sasterawan Perancis sudah tertarik dengannya? Pada tahun 1829, Victor Hugo, pengarang Les Misérables, memperkenalkan pantun berkait Melayu menerusi antologi puisinya, Les Orientales. Bentuk puisi ini kemudian diadaptasi oleh penyair Perancis sehingga dikenali sebagai pantoum.

Bayangkan, ketika orang Eropah sedang meneroka keunikan struktur puisi warisan kita, nenek moyang kita sudah menjadikannya sebahagian daripada cara mereka berkomunikasi dalam kehidupan seharian. Sayang sekali jika kita hanya mewarisi pantunnya tetapi tidak mewarisi kecerdasan berfikir yang melahirkan pantun itu. Dan dalam bab ini, saya menghargai kegemaran Ahmad Maslan berpantun. Agak-agak bernas atau tidak cadangan saya agar kemahiran berpantun diajar secara serius di sekolah?

af2379ca2419bb97: The leaders of the great model houses, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, desperately want the world to believe AI is the skeleton key which will unlock the secrets of the universe.
But if the AI can’t explain what it’s “proven,” are we actually any closer to understanding anything, or have we simply built another black box?

That question is top of mind among mathematicians and computer scientists this week after Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved a mathematical conjecture so elusive it's gone unproven for more than 150 years. The fact that this note came out one day after Anthropic's record-setting IPO is a coincidence, we're sure.

In a four-page post to his website, the researcher described how with the help of Claude, he believes he has proven the Riemann Hypothesis, one of seven Millennium problems so complex and so important that the Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize to anyone who is successful in solving them.

The Riemann Hypothesis, conjectured by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, contends that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function – those with a real part between zero and one – have a real part equal to 1/2.

Confused? Don’t worry. We’ve linked to an explainer that goes into more detail here. What's important is that, if the Riemann Hypothesis is right, mathematicians can place tighter bounds on the difference between the actual distribution of prime numbers and mathematical estimates of that distribution.

Researchers have previously attempted to disprove the conjecture through computational brute force, and therein have shown the hypothesis holds to at least 10 trillion zeros. There’s reason to believe that the Riemann Hypothesis is accurate, but the possibility remains that over a sufficiently long series the pattern might diverge. And so, more than 150 years after Riemann published his hypothesis, it has remained just that.
Alpöge’s proof, if it can even be called that, is now the subject of great debate.

The four pages in which Alpöge remarks on the discoveries he and Claude made aren’t exactly a proof, but rather 14 tarballs worth of Lean code totaling roughly 240 MB. Lean is an open source programming language commonly used to help validate mathematical proofs.

The Clay Mathematics Institute, which oversees the seven Millennium Problems, has promoted the Riemann Hypothesis from “unsolved” to “active” status, but it is not yet considered solved. For Clay to consider the problem solved and award the prize, the proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, remain available for scrutiny for at least two years, and receive broad acceptance from the mathematics community.
As it stands, Alpöge describes the 250,000 pages of text generated by the model for its written proof as a “massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop.’”

Not long after Alpöge's remarks and Lean code were published, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil released a nearly 1,000-page draft proof by Alessandro Maria Masullo, who earned his PhD at Stanford in 2020. Masullo has reportedly spent more than a decade pursuing the problem.

Frameworks like Lean make mathematics a prime candidate for AI-assisted discovery for many of the same reasons that the technology has proven so successful in software development: code either compiles and runs or it doesn’t.

Code can also be audited and could, with great effort, be deciphered. But a proof written in Lean isn't a mathematical proof in the traditional, human-readable sense. Although its logical validity can be checked by a computer, understanding the reasoning behind it can be another matter. Traditional proofs ideally explain their arguments in a way that other mathematicians can follow. Cantor's Diagonal Argument offers a comparatively accessible example.
While the clock hasn’t even started for the Clay Math Institute, the Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative have already declared the Riemann Hypothesis solved.

“We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the orgs wrote in a joint statement. “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.”
Even if the code ends up being right, if we still don’t know why it’s true, have we really learned anything meaningful?
"At the minute, we don't even know why the theorem is true," Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said in a recent Al Jazeera interview.
Alpöge’s proof may simply be the product of a black box. To quote the late Arthur C Clarke, “any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.”
The implications of such a technology aren’t lost on researchers. Months ago, several prominent researchers called for greater scrutiny and oversight regarding the application of AI in mathematics.

“Mathematics produces not only a body of results, but also understanding, clarity, and judgment among the communities of mathematicians who have shaped them, often in the context of their own autonomously guided research,” the Leiden Declaration reads. “This expert knowledge is essential, both to effectively use mathematics, and to continue to articulate new and significant research questions.” ®

7936a1d5242e0abf: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 24 — Malaysia must ensure that its newly elevated strategic partnership with France translates into meaningful technology transfer and industrial development, rather than relegating the country to a supplier of raw materials for Europe’s strategic ambitions, said Citizens International executive director Imran Mohd Rasid.

He said closer cooperation with France could help Malaysia diversify its economy and strengthen its industrial capabilities, but cautioned against agreements that could create new forms of economic dependence.

“Malaysia must avoid becoming a mineral supplier for somebody else’s industrial revolution. We should welcome French investment, but Malaysia must not exchange one form of dependency for another,” he said.

His remarks follow French President Emmanuel Macron’s two-day official visit to Malaysia on November 16 and 17, during which both countries elevated bilateral relations to a Strategic Partnership encompassing critical minerals, defence, energy and advanced technologies.

Among the key developments was a rare earth industrial project involving French company Carester and Malaysia’s Malaco Mining Group, which is expected to begin operations in early 2027. The project will involve extraction and processing in Malaysia, with further refining to be carried out in France.

Imran, who is also an international relations expert specialising in Global South affairs, said the arrangement could benefit Malaysia if it enabled the country to move beyond supplying raw materials and develop its own high-value industries.
“If France wants access to our rare earths, it should also help Malaysia acquire the technology, knowledge and industrial capabilities to become a producer of higher-value products,” he said.

He stressed that Malaysia should sweek substantive technology transfer, greater participation by local companies in separation, refining and downstream manufacturing, and opportunities for Malaysian workers and suppliers to undertake higher-value activities.
He also cautioned against environmental risks associated with rare earth extraction and processing, particularly waste management and pollution.

The Malaysian government has maintained its moratorium on raw rare earth exports, which took effect on Jan 1, 2024, while allowing limited and conditional exports for research, development and processing purposes.

Deputy Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Syed Ibrahim Syed Noh told the Dewan Rakyat on Thursday that cooperation with France would focus on technological expertise and developing the entire rare earth value chain, from mining and processing to high-value products.

Imran said the timing of Macron’s visit also reflected growing European concerns over strategic vulnerabilities, with the war in Ukraine, energy insecurity and geopolitical tensions exposing Europe’s dependence on external suppliers for critical minerals, energy and technology.
He said Europe’s growing interest in the Global South could give developing countries greater bargaining power.
On the shared emphasis by Malaysia and France on strategic autonomy, Imran said the concept must be understood in the context of their vastly different economic and geopolitical positions.

He said while France viewed strategic autonomy primarily as a means of protecting its international position and reducing vulnerabilities, Malaysia needed to pursue it as a strategy to overcome structural economic dependencies and strengthen its own development capabilities. — Bernama
